detail.what: read the goal's snr_target as target_relative_error, so x_min = sigma_loc/target looked like it had its target
detail.why_wrong: an SNR target is about detecting the bead; x_min is about resolving how far it was pushed. They are different quantities and one does not stand in for the other

detail.what: wrote kb_refs as strings of the form kb:<entry_id>

detail.shape_to_remember: one wrong sibling field produced five findings: a failing subschema contributes no annotations, so unevaluatedProperties then reports every field common_head would have covered as unexpected. A cascade of unevaluated-property errors on a card that plainly has those fields means one sibling is the wrong shape

detail.caught_by: this seat's own to_card(), against the contract; no validator ran

detail.what: A4 for widefield_inline ran on the normal path, produced five outcomes, and could not be written as a card
detail.how_far_it_got: the service answered: five entries returned with their own grades and five questions returned absent, all stamped answered_from kbv-49feb73662b7 at commit 9baf01d, and the served digests matched that commit's blobs byte for byte. degraded would have been empty and true -- the first time in this repository. Three of five bounds abstain no_input and two return.
detail.why_no_card: axis.schema.json makes `interval` required when a ledger entry's state is `returned`, and common.schema.json's interval requires {parameter, unit, basis} with numeric min/max and forbids additional properties. A4's two returning bounds constrain plan FORM, not a number: name the selector as an element rather than a channel, and establish the loaded state by acquiring rather than by read-back. There is no shape in the contract for a bound that has grounds and is not numeric.
detail.why_not_worked_around: all three alternatives misreport. A fabricated interval would rest on an empty `basis`, and basis names entries in numbers[] which A4 has none of -- a bound resting on nothing. And each abstention kind is false: the inputs were present (not no_input), the bound bites (not not_constraining), and it was asked for (not not_requested). 4.5.2.1 refuses silence; it does not ask for a wrong word instead.
detail.what_would_clear_it: a slot for a discrete constraint in axis.schema.json, which is contracts/ and the manager's (6.2). axis_common.returned_needs_numeric_interval() reads the rule off the schema, so the refusal clears itself when the slot exists; the axis module and the ledger are committed and re-running it emits the card.
detail.shape_to_remember: the axis ledger was designed by axes that bound numbers. A1 bounds exposure time, A7 bounds a velocity -- both numeric, both fit. A4 is the first axis whose answers are discrete, and the contract's three outcome shapes were complete only for the axes that had been written. A vocabulary that fits every case so far is not the same as a vocabulary that fits.

detail.what: kb_query was called with an entry_id in the observable slot, and the answer it produced reads in the log as a mismatch the card ignored
detail.what_came_back: the entry, in returned[], at E3 -- and alongside it coverage {'stand_ti2e_lock_groups': 'no_overlap'} and gaps ['condition_mismatch']
detail.why_it_was_called: at this pin an entry is reachable only by an id the caller already knows: `subject` was added to the entries after kbv-49feb73662b7, and the server offers no tool that lists ids. This was a probe of whether kb_query would match by id, before falling back to kb_get.
detail.why_the_conclusion_still_stands: the entry was cited from kb_get, which returns it verbatim with its digest, and the digest was checked byte for byte against the pinned commit's blob. The E3 the card records is the entry's own grade. Nothing in the card rests on this call.
detail.why_it_needed_a_record_anyway: the log now holds a condition_mismatch against an entry the card cites at E3, and nothing on disk explains it. Anyone running the 0.3-4 cross-check mechanically -- a person or a later check -- reads that as the card having ignored a mismatch. The record is the only thing standing between that signal and that reading.
detail.what_the_no_overlap_actually_meant: not that the entry is unfit. kb_entry.schema.json rules that an entry with no machine-readable `validity` comes back as overlap no_overlap rather than matching silently, and this entry carries prose validity_conditions and no `validity`. So the verdict was about the absence of a field to compare against, and condition_range was null -- no condition was asked about at all. The same rule produced yesterday's tau_d near-miss re-read on goal.json, where it was also the real reason and also not the obvious one.
detail.structural_half_not_ours: the log keeps one `observable` column and it holds two kinds of name -- an observable for kb_query, an entry_id for kb_get. manager-microscope had already raised that with architecture as a hypothesis about joins going wrong; this call is the first instance of the false signal it predicted, and that seat is carrying the demonstration up.
detail.shape_to_remember: put an entry_id in kb_query's `observable` and the service answers no_overlap, which reads as 'unfit' and means 'this is not an observable, and there is no validity to compare'. The entry comes back anyway, so the call looks successful while leaving a mismatch in the log. Use kb_get when you have an id, and record the probe if you do it the other way.

detail.what: the same wrong call was made again under a2 -- an entry_id in kb_query's observable slot -- and repeating it is what showed the problem is not the call
detail.what_came_back: the entry at E4 in returned[], and alongside it coverage no_overlap with a condition_mismatch gap -- the same pair as the 07:26:33 call on stand_ti2e_lock_groups recorded an hour earlier
detail.why_it_repeated: no excuse worth recording: this seat had written the shape_to_remember for exactly this an hour before and reached for kb_query anyway. tau_d is a symbol as well as an id, which makes the call defensible and did not make it right -- kb_get was the tool and was used immediately after.
detail.the_measurement_that_matters: 17 of the 25 entries in the store carry no machine-readable `validity` -- only the 6 objectives, the coverslip thickness and the water viscosity do. kb_entry.schema.json rules that an entry without `validity` comes back as overlap no_overlap rather than matching silently. So kb_query answers condition_mismatch for 68% of the store no matter how it is asked, and the two instances logged today are the default behaviour rather than two mistakes.
detail.why_that_is_worse_than_a_bad_call: 0.3-4 makes the query log the way to check whether a card's `degraded` is honest, and that check has just become runnable. Run mechanically against this store it would read a condition_mismatch against a correctly cited entry as the card having ignored a mismatch, on 17 of 25 entries. The rule itself is right -- the schema says `rather than matching silently` and means it, so a caller cannot get a false silent match. What is missing is that `kind` has one word for two situations: a mismatch because the asked conditions genuinely fall outside an entry's validity, and a mismatch because there is no machine-readable validity to compare against. Only the first says anything about fitness.
detail.what_would_clear_it: either a `kind` that separates the two -- no_validity_declared as against condition_mismatch -- or `validity` on the other 17 entries. Both are the librarian's and the contract's, not this seat's. Named here because A2 and A4 are the first two cards whose honesty the log will be used to check.
detail.shape_to_remember: a record written to stop a repeat did not stop the repeat, and that is the second finding. The first record said `use kb_get when you have an id`, which is advice about a call; what the caller needed was the reason the answer is misleading, which is a property of the store. Advice not to do a thing is weaker than knowing why the thing looks like it worked.
